manifest.summaryEvidence: My most recent visit to Israel overlapped with its election in October, but that was a coincidence. At times he seemed to symbolize Israel itself, in which life and death are close partners.” I had visited Israel in November 2023, while the horrors of the Hamas onslaught were still fresh—more than 800 civilians and 300 soldiers killed, 251 hostages seized. I saw the room where one disabled old woman had been burned alive in bed; the house where a father was killed in front of his children, the scattered toys and playthings. Only the bloodstains had, in accordance with Jewish ritual, been painstakingly removed. It was a country in deep and open trauma. The trauma is no longer on the surface. The trauma, however, is now like an artesian river: running below the surface, but immensely powerful. The election offered proof of that. It didn’t take long after Trump’s second win for Leyva to realize that he had been duped. First, he said, Trump seemed to obstruct the release of the Epstein files, which didn’t live up to the MAGA-sphere hype when some of them were finally made public. Then the president did something he had said he wasn’t going to do: start a war. Leyva now spends nearly twice as much on gas as he did last year—sometimes it costs him $300 a week. I ran into him outside a home-improvement store in Scottsdale, where voters will decide one of the nation’s competitive congressional races. I asked whether he was planning to vote. “Hell no.
